headline: Open-Source AWS Security Tool for solo devs & founders launched
summary: Plexavo scans IAM, S3, EC2, and networking for misconfigurations, providing a score and actionable fixes.
details: Solo developers and founders managing their own AWS accounts often lack dedicated security teams. Plexavo is an open-source tool designed to address this gap, scanning for misconfigurations and potential privilege escalation paths within IAM, S3, EC2, and networking services.

The tool provides a security score from 0-100 and generates a plain-English report detailing identified issues, their potential impact, and the exact commands needed to fix them. It runs locally using your own credentials, ensuring zero telemetry and that no data leaves your machine.

Plexavo's detection logic is built on pure Python and boto3, avoiding AI-driven hallucinated findings. While an optional AI layer can be used to rephrase findings in simpler terms, it does not influence the identification of security issues and is fully opt-in.

Currently at version v0.1.2, Plexavo welcomes contributions through issues and pull requests. The deterministic nature of its checks allows for code auditing, providing transparency into its operations.

The project emphasizes privacy and security, with all scans performed locally. Users are encouraged to run the tool against their own accounts and provide feedback, with the developer prioritizing genuine findings and bug reports over stars.

headline_marked: Smartphone cameras aren't [[truly RAW]] — here's why it's problematic
headline: Smartphone cameras aren't truly RAW — here's why it's problematic
summary: While many phones boast RAW photo capabilities, the reality is often more complex, leading to issues with true RAW data.
details: Many smartphones advertise shooting in RAW format, promising photographers ultimate control over their images. However, the term 'RAW' in the context of smartphone cameras is often misleading.

Unlike professional cameras that capture unprocessed sensor data, smartphone RAW files frequently undergo some level of in-camera processing. This can include noise reduction, sharpening, and color adjustments, meaning they aren't truly 'raw' in the traditional sense.

This processing can limit the flexibility and quality that users expect from RAW files. Adjustments made in-camera are baked in, and attempting to reverse them or apply new edits can lead to artifacts and a degradation of image quality.

The issue stems from the complex computational photography techniques employed by modern smartphones. These processes, while improving everyday photos, complicate the capture of pure, unadulterated sensor data.
For users seeking genuine RAW capabilities for advanced editing, the current implementation on most smartphones can be problematic, falling short of the professional standard.
